# Core


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Create an app with `app = FastHTML()`. The `@rt` decorator adds routes
(`rt = app.route`), inferring what it can from the function:

    @rt
    def index(): ...      # GET,POST /
    @rt
    def foo(): ...        # GET,POST /foo
    @rt('/hi')
    def get(): ...        # GET /hi (function named after a verb handles just that verb)
    @rt('/cards/{id}')
    class Cards: ...      # class route group: each verb-named method (get, patch, ...) becomes a handler

The decorated function doubles as a URL builder, so links never need
hardcoded paths:

    A('More', href=foo.to(a=1))   # <a href="/foo?a=1"> `.to()` fills path params; the rest become query params.
    Div('...', hx_get=foo)        # route functions work directly as htmx attr values: hx-get="/foo"

Handlers return FT trees (from `fastcore.xml`), rendered as HTML
automatically: a full page for regular requests, a bare fragment for
HTMX requests. In a full page, top-level `Title`, `Meta`, `Link`, and
`Style` items go in `<head>`; the rest goes in `<body>`. Strings are
sent as HTML, dicts as JSON, and a Starlette `Response` is sent
untouched. A return tuple may mix content with special items: any
`HttpHeader` (e.g. from `cookie()` or `HtmxResponseHeaders()`) becomes a
response header, any `BackgroundTask` runs after the response is sent,
and the rest renders as content. `Redirect` picks the right redirect
mechanism for HTMX vs regular requests, and `FtResponse` wraps FT
content when you need the status code or headers.

Handler parameters are filled from the request: each is looked up in
path, cookie, header (snake_case names match Hyphen-Case headers),
query, then form data, and cast by calling its annotation on the value.
Hyphens in form/query names match underscores in handler parameters and
typed body fields. Exact names take precedence within each source.
Dictionary and request access retain the original keys. `bool`, `int`,
and `date` get smart string parsing; `UploadFile` passes through.
Repeated params take the last value unless annotated `list[T]`, which
collects them all. A param with no annotation and no special name is
ignored, with a warning. A dataclass, TypedDict, namedtuple, or any
annotated class collects the whole form body; a `__from_request__`
classmethod customizes construction. A missing required param is a 400,
a failed cast a 404. These special names need no annotation:

    req, ws   the Request / WebSocket connection
    sess      session dict
    app       the FastHTML app
    state     app.state
    scope     ASGI scope
    auth      scope['auth']
    htmx      HtmxHeaders (parsed HX-* request headers)
    body      raw body text
    data      parsed form data as a dict
    api       ApiReturn (API vs browser dual responses)
    send      websocket send function
    hdrs,ftrs the per-request copies of the app's `hdrs`/`ftrs` (head and footer content)
    htmlkw    the per-request copy of the app's `<html>` attrs
    bodykw    the per-request copy of the app's `<body>` attrs
    resp      the handler's response (injected into `after` functions)

`before`/`after` functions (app-level, with `Beforeware` skip patterns,
or per-route `before=`) get the same param injection as handlers. A
`before` returning a value responds with it and skips the handler (the
usual auth-guard pattern).

See the [Handling Handlers
tutorial](https://www.fastht.ml/docs/ref/handlers.html.md) for worked
examples of the above.

This is the source code to fasthtml. You won’t need to read this unless
you want to understand how things are built behind the scenes, or need
full details of a particular API. The notebook is converted to the
Python module
[fasthtml/core.py](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fasthtml/blob/main/fasthtml/core.py)
using [nbdev](https://nbdev.fast.ai/).

``` python
def test_request(url: str='/', headers: dict=None, method: str='get')->Request:
    if headers is None: headers={}
    scope = dict(type='http', method=method, path=url, headers=Headers(headers).raw, query_string=b'', scheme='http',
        client=('127.0.0.1', 8000), server=('127.0.0.1', 8000))
    async def receive(): return dict(type="http.request", body=b"", more_body=False)
    return Request(scope, receive)
```

### ApiReturn

``` python
def ApiReturn(
    isapi:bool=False
):
```

*Request param: call with browser and API responses; returns kwargs as
JSON if the client accepts `application/json`, else `norm`*

Routes often need to return different responses depending on whether the
request comes from a browser or an API client. The `api:ApiReturn`
parameter handles this automatically — add it to any route signature and
call it with two arguments: the API response and the browser response.
If the request’s `Accept` header is `application/json` then a dict of
the kwargs is returned, otherwise, the first value is returned. For
example, `return api(Redirect('/records'), id=record.id)` returns
{‘id’:id} for API callers and a redirect for the browser. This keeps
your route logic in one place instead of splitting it across separate
endpoints.

### JSONResponse

``` python
def JSONResponse(
    content:Any, status_code:int=200, headers:Mapping[str, str] | None=None, media_type:str | None=None,
    background:BackgroundTask | None=None
)->None:
```

*Same as starlette’s version, but auto-stringifies non serializable
types*

``` python
async def f(req):
    def _f(p:HttpHeader): ...
    p = first(_params(_f).values())
    data = form2dict(await parse_form(req))
    result = await _from_body(req, p, data)
    return JSONResponse(result.__dict__)

client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[Route('/', f, methods=['POST'])]))

d = dict(k='value1',v=['value2','value3'])
response = client.post('/', data=d)
print(response.json())
```

    {'k': 'value1', 'v': 'value3'}

``` python
# An empty `application/json` body yields `{}` (like the empty-multipart guard), not a 500
async def _empty_json(req): return JSONResponse(form2dict(await parse_form(req)))
client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[Route('/', _empty_json, methods=['POST'])]))
res = client.post('/', headers={'content-type':'application/json'})
test_eq(res.status_code, 200)
test_eq(res.json(), {})
res = client.post('/', json={'a':1})          # non-empty json still parses (behavior preserved)
test_eq(res.json(), {'a':1})
```

A malformed multipart body (here the opening boundary isn’t followed by
CRLF) is the client’s error, so `parse_form` answers 400 rather than
letting the parser’s exception surface as a 500:

``` python
bad = b'--xyzXX\r\nContent-Disposition: form-data; name="a"\r\n\r\n1\r\n--xyz--\r\n'
res = client.post('/', content=bad, headers={'content-type':'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'})
test_eq(res.status_code, 400)
res.text
```

A JSON body that does not decode, or decodes to something other than an
object (an array, say), cannot supply route parameters, so it is refused
with 400 rather than failing inside the form conversion:

``` python
res = client.post('/', json=[1,2])
test_eq(res.status_code, 400)
res = client.post('/', content=b'not json', headers={'content-type':'application/json'})
test_eq(res.status_code, 400)
res.text
```

``` python
client.get('/?x=1&x=2').text
```

``` python
class Bar(BasicRepr):
    @classmethod
    def __from_request__(cls, accept:str=None): return cls(accept)
    def __init__(self, accept): self.accept = accept

def g(b:Bar): ...

async def f(req):
    result = await _wrap_req(req, _params(g))
    return Response(repr(result['b']))

client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[Route('/', f, methods=['POST'])]))
client.post('/', headers={'Accept': 'application/json'}).text
```

    "Bar(accept='application/json')"

**Missing Request Params**

If a request param has a default value (e.g. `a:str=''`), the request is
valid even if the user doesn’t include the param in their request.

``` python
def g(req, this:Starlette, a:str=''): ...

async def f(req):
    a = await _wrap_req(req, _params(g))
    return Response(str(a))

client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[Route('/', f, methods=['POST'])]))
response = client.post('/', json={}) # no param in request
print(response.text)
```

    {'req': <starlette.requests.Request object>, 'this': <starlette.applications.Starlette object>, 'a': ''}

If we remove the default value and re-run the request, we should get the
following error `Missing required field: a`.

``` python
def g(req, this:Starlette, a:str): ...

async def f(req):
    a = await _wrap_req(req, _params(g))
    return Response(str(a))

client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[Route('/', f, methods=['POST'])]))
response = client.post('/', json={}) # no param in request
print(response.text)
```

    Missing required field: a

## Websockets / SSE

``` python
def on_receive(msg:str): return f"Message text was: {msg}"
c = _ws_endp(on_receive)
cli = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[WebSocketRoute('/', _ws_endp(on_receive))]))
with cli.websocket_connect('/') as ws:
    ws.send_text('{"msg":"Hi!"}')
    data = ws.receive_text()
    assert data == 'Message text was: Hi!', data
```

``` python
def on_receive(hx_trigger:str): return f"trigger: {hx_trigger}"
cli = TestClient(Starlette(routes=[WebSocketRoute('/', _ws_endp(on_receive))]))
with cli.websocket_connect('/') as ws:
    ws.send_text(json.dumps({"HEADERS": {"Hx-Trigger": "my-btn"}}))
    data = ws.receive_text()
    assert data == 'trigger: my-btn', data
```

### qp

``` python
def qp(
    p:str, **kw
)->str:
```

*Add parameters kw to path p*

`qp` adds query parameters to route path strings

``` python
vals = dict(a=5, b=False, c=[1,2], d='bar', e=None, ab=42)
```

``` python
res = qp('/foo', **vals)
test_eq(res, '/foo?a=5&b=&c=1&c=2&d=bar&e=&ab=42')
```

`qp` checks to see if each param should be sent as a query parameter or
as part of the route, and encodes that properly.

``` python
path = '/foo/{a}/{d}/{ab:int}'
res = qp(path, **vals)
test_eq(res, '/foo/5/bar/42?b=&c=1&c=2&e=')
```

### HostRoute

``` python
def HostRoute(
    path, endpoint, *, host:NoneType=None, **kwargs
):
```

*Route with optional host-header constraint using Starlette’s {param}
pattern syntax*

``` python
app = FastHTML()
app.router.routes = []

app.router.routes.append(HostRoute('/', lambda _: Response('auth page'), host='auth.{parentdom}', methods=['GET'], name='auth_home'))
app.router.routes.append(HostRoute('/', lambda _: Response('main page'), methods=['GET'], name='main_home'))

cli = TestClient(app)
test_eq(cli.get('/', headers={'host': 'auth.localhost'}).text, 'auth page')
test_eq(cli.get('/', headers={'host': 'localhost'}).text, 'main page')
test_eq(cli.get('/', headers={'host': 'auth.example.com'}).text, 'auth page')
print('all passed')
```

    all passed

``` python
app.router.routes.append(HostRoute('/hello', lambda _: Response('api hello'), host='api.{parentdom}', methods=['GET'], name='api_hello'))
app.router.routes.append(HostRoute('/hello', lambda _: Response('normal hello'), methods=['GET'], name='hello'))

test_eq(cli.get('/hello', headers={'host': 'api.mysite.com'}).text, 'api hello')
test_eq(cli.get('/hello', headers={'host': 'mysite.com'}).text, 'normal hello')
test_eq(cli.get('/hello', headers={'host': 'other.mysite.com'}).text, 'normal hello')
print('all passed')
```

    all passed

### serve

``` python
def serve(
    appname:NoneType=None, # Name of the module
    app:str='app', # App instance to be served
    host:str='0.0.0.0', # If host is 0.0.0.0 will convert to localhost
    port:NoneType=None, # If port is None it will default to 5001 or the PORT environment variable
    reload:bool=True, # Default is to reload the app upon code changes
    procs:NoneType=None, # Processes to run on consecutive ports from `port`; default 1 or the PROCS environment variable
    **kwargs
):
```

*Run the app in an async server, with live reload set as the default.*

`procs` runs the app as that many processes on consecutive ports from
`port`, each with its own reload supervisor, and defaults to the `PROCS`
environment variable. `serve` re-executes the script once per process
with `FH_PROCNUM` set to its number, which is also the guard against a
child spawning again. An app reads `FH_PROCNUM` for work that only one
process should do, such as a background job: it is `'0'` in the first
process, and unset in an ordinary single-process run. A reverse proxy in
front of the ports decides how requests reach them.

Starlette does not cancel a running handler when a client disconnects:
the disconnect is only visible as an `http.disconnect` message on the
ASGI receive channel, which ordinary handlers never read.
`until_disconnect` races a coroutine against that message, cancelling
the work if the client goes away first.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### until_disconnect

``` python
async def until_disconnect(
    req, coro
):
```

*Await `coro`, cancelling it (and returning an empty response) if the
client disconnects first*

`cancel_on_disconnect` applies this to a route handler. `splice_sig`
adds a private `Request`-annotated parameter to the exposed signature,
which FastHTML fills with the connection, so the handler’s own
parameters are unchanged. It requires an async handler, since a sync
handler runs in a threadpool and cannot be cancelled.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### cancel_on_disconnect

``` python
def cancel_on_disconnect(
    f:NoneType=None, # Async route handler to wrap
    *, timeout:NoneType=None, # Also cancel the handler after this many seconds
):
```

*Route decorator: cancel the handler when the client disconnects*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Client

``` python
def Client(
    app, url:str='http://testserver'
):
```

*A simple httpx ASGI client that doesn’t require `async`*

``` python
app = FastHTML(routes=[Route('/', lambda _: Response('test'))])
cli = Client(app)

cli.get('/').text
```

    'test'

Note that you can also use Starlette’s `TestClient` instead of
FastHTML’s `Client`. They should be largely interchangable.

``` python
# Modified toast functions to test resp logic
def toast_after_(resp, req, sess):
    if sk in sess and (not resp or isinstance(resp, (tuple,FT,FtResponse))):
        sess['toast_duration'] = req.app.state.toast_duration
        # We will activate the toast depending on the content of the response
        if str('love') in str(resp): req.injects.append(render_toasts(sess))

def setup_toasts_(app, duration=5000):
    app.state.toast_duration = duration
    app.hdrs += [Style(toast_css), Script(js)]
    app.after.append(toast_after_)
```

A route-level `before` can set session data, short-circuit with a
response, or raise to block access:

``` python
def check_user(sess, user:str=''):
    if user == 'admin':
        sess['foo'] = 'bar'
        return None
    if user == 'guest': return 'guest view'
    raise HTTPException(403, 'forbidden')

@rt('/dashboard', before=check_user)
def get(sess): return sess.get('foo')

test_eq(cli.get('/dashboard?user=admin').text, 'bar')
test_eq(cli.get('/dashboard?user=guest').text, 'guest view')
test_eq(cli.get('/dashboard?user=other').status_code, 403)
```

Multiple `before` functions run in order, each receiving the injected
request params:

``` python
def set_a(sess): sess['a'] = 1
def set_b(sess): sess['b'] = 2

@rt('/multi', before=(set_a, set_b))
def get(sess): return f"{sess.get('a')},{sess.get('b')}"

test_eq(cli.get('/multi').text, '1,2')
```

A truthy return from any `before` becomes the response; remaining
`before`s and the handler are skipped (return `None` to continue):

``` python
calls = []
def first(sess): 
    calls.append('first')
    return 'stop'
def second(sess): calls.append('second')

@rt('/chain', before=(first, second))
def get(sess): return 'handler'

test_eq(cli.get('/chain').text, 'stop')
test_eq(calls, ['first'])
```

`cancel_on_disconnect` handlers keep their normal parameters; the
handler is cancelled if the client disconnects, or after `timeout`
seconds if given:

``` python
app,cli,rt = get_cli(FastHTML())

@rt('/cq')
@cancel_on_disconnect
async def cq(q:str): return f'got {q}'

test_eq(cli.get('/cq?q=x').text, 'got x')
```

``` python
@rt('/sleepy')
@cancel_on_disconnect(timeout=0.01)
async def sleepy():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return 'nope'

test_fail(lambda: cli.get('/sleepy'))
```

On disconnect the handler is cancelled and an empty response returned,
which the server discards since the client is gone. Here we simulate the
ASGI `http.disconnect` message directly:

``` python
async def _disc(): return {'type': 'http.disconnect'}
cancelled = []
async def _work():
    try: await asyncio.sleep(10)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        cancelled.append(True)
        raise

async def _t():
    scope = dict(type='http', method='GET', path='/', query_string=b'', headers=[])
    res = await until_disconnect(Request(scope, _disc), _work())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return res

test_eq(run_sync(_t()).status_code, 204)
test_eq(cancelled, [True])
```

``` python
@ar("/hi")
def get(): return 'Hi there'
@ar("/hi")
def post(): return 'Postal'
@ar
def ho(): return 'Ho ho'
@ar("/hostie")
def show_host(req): return req.headers['host']
@ar
def yoyo(): return 'a yoyo'
@ar
def index(): return "home page"
@ar('/class-cards/{id}')
class CardMethods:
    async def get(id:str): return f'get {id}'
    async def patch(card:Card): return asdict(card)
    async def delete(id:str): return f'delete {id}'


@ar.ws("/ws")
def ws(self, msg:str): return f"Message text was: {msg}"
```

``` python

ar.to_app(app)
```

``` python

# ensure route functions are properly discoverable on `APIRouter` and `APIRouter.rt_funcs`
assert ar.prefix == ''
assert str(ar.rt_funcs.index) == '/'
assert str(ar.index) == '/'
with ExceptionExpected(): ar.blah()
with ExceptionExpected(): ar.rt_funcs.blah()
# ensure any route functions named using an HTTPMethod are not discoverable via `rt_funcs`
assert "get" not in ar.rt_funcs._funcs.keys()
```

### StaticNoCache

``` python
def StaticNoCache(
    *, directory:PathLike | None=None, packages:list[str | tuple[str, str]] | None=None, html:bool=False,
    check_dir:bool=True, follow_symlink:bool=False
)->None:
```

*StaticFiles that sends `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so browsers
revalidate on every use*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### StaticImmutable

``` python
def StaticImmutable(
    *, directory:PathLike | None=None, packages:list[str | tuple[str, str]] | None=None, html:bool=False,
    check_dir:bool=True, follow_symlink:bool=False
)->None:
```

*Like `StaticNoCache`, but marks responses as cacheable forever: for
versioned URLs such as `vurl` links or content-hashed filenames*

These two classes are the poles of static-file caching. `StaticNoCache`
makes the browser revalidate on every use: always fresh at the cost of a
conditional request each time, right for files that change under a
stable URL (and for dev, where you want edits visible on reload).
`StaticImmutable` promises the URL’s content will never change, so the
browser may cache it forever with no requests at all: only safe when a
changed file gets a changed URL, which is what `vurl` or a bundler’s
content-hashed filenames provide.

``` python
statd = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(statd/'app.css').write_text('body{}')
stat_app = FastHTML(routes=[Mount('/nc', StaticNoCache(directory=statd)), Mount('/imm', StaticImmutable(directory=statd))])
stat_cli = TestClient(stat_app)
test_eq(stat_cli.get('/nc/app.css').headers['cache-control'], 'no-cache')
test_eq(stat_cli.get('/imm/app.css').headers['cache-control'], 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable')
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### vurl

``` python
def vurl(
    path, root:str='.'
):
```

*Return `path` as a URL with a `v` query param hashing the file’s
contents, so the URL changes when the file does*

Browsers use the URL as the cache key, so a URL that changes whenever
the file’s contents change can be cached forever: serve the mount with
`StaticImmutable` and the asset costs no requests at all until it is
next edited. This is the query-param version of the content-hashed
filenames that asset pipelines and bundlers produce, without the build
step. The hash is cached via `flexicache` with `mtime_policy`, so a call
costs one `stat` and the file is only re-read after it changes. The
param is inert under `no-cache` serving, so the same links work in dev
with `StaticNoCache`, where the file is rechecked on each reload.

``` python
tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(tmp/'a.css').write_text('body{}')
u = vurl('a.css', tmp)
assert u.startswith('a.css?v=')
test_eq(u, vurl('a.css', tmp))
test_eq(vurl('/a.css', tmp).split('?')[0], '/a.css')
q = vurl('/a.css?theme=dark#top', tmp)
assert q.startswith('/a.css?theme=dark&v=') and q.endswith('#top')
(tmp/'a.css').write_text('body{color:red}')
os.utime(tmp/'a.css', (time.time()+1,)*2)
assert vurl('a.css', tmp) != u
```

### into

``` python
def into(
    func
):
```

*Decorator to pass a route’s return value into `func`, with keyword
params added to the route signature*

`into` is a decorator that composes two functions: the decorated route
function and an outer “wrapper” function (like a layout). The route’s
return value is passed as positional args to the wrapper. Any keyword
parameters listed in `params` are added to the route’s signature, so
they become available as query/form parameters. This lets you write
simple routes that return just their content, while the layout and its
parameters are handled automatically.

Here `hello` returns a single `P` tag, but `into(my_layout)` passes it
into `my_layout`, which wraps it in a `Titled`. The `title` parameter is
injected into `hello`’s signature so it can be set via query params.

``` python
app,cli,rt = get_cli(FastHTML())

def my_layout(*c, title:str='Default'): return Titled(title, *c)

@rt
@into(my_layout)
def hello(name:str='World'): return P(f'Hello, {name}!')
```

With no query params, `name` defaults to `'World'` and `title` defaults
to `'Default'` (from `my_layout`’s own default), giving us a page titled
“Default” containing “Hello, World!”.

``` python
r = cli.get('/hello')
assert '<title>Default</title>' in r.text
assert '<p>Hello, World!</p>' in r.text
```

Here, both `name` and `title` are provided as query params.
`name='Jeremy'` is handled by `hello` directly, while
`title='Greetings'` is the injected param that gets forwarded to
`my_layout`.

``` python
r = cli.get('/hello?name=Jeremy&title=Greetings')
assert '<title>Greetings</title>' in r.text
assert '<p>Hello, Jeremy!</p>' in r.text
```

``` python
def backgrounds():

    for i in range(3): tasks.add_task(increment, i)
    return P('BG Tasks'), tasks
```
